restatements.text: Titles the measure the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.
Outlines findings regarding funding challenges for Medi-Cal, public education, and food assistance programs, and notes the accumulated wealth of billionaires in California.
States the purpose of the act is to raise revenue for health care, education, and food assistance through a one-time tax on billionaire wealth.

Amends the California Constitution to authorize the one-time wealth tax on billionaires, establishes a Reserve Fund exempt from standard appropriations limits, and sets allocations of 90% for health and 10% for education and food assistance.

Directs how the Reserve Fund shall be allocated, provides a $50 million start-up loan to the Franchise Tax Board, mandates reporting to the Legislature, and prohibits using the new funds to supplant existing state spending.

Establishes a 5% excise tax on the net worth of individuals over $1 billion for the 2026 tax year. Details rules for valuing private businesses and trusts, excludes directly held real estate and certain retirement accounts, and outlines penalties, enforcement powers, and expedited judicial review.
Prohibits taxpayers from taking a deduction for the new net worth tax.
Provides that if this measure receives more votes than a conflicting measure regarding a billionaire net worth tax, this measure shall prevail.
Authorizes the proponent or any citizen to defend the act in court if the Attorney General does not.

analysis.answer: Current law was not provided. The measure creates a one-time 5% excise tax in 2026 on the net worth of California residents exceeding $1 billion. It exempts directly held real estate and caps the application for certain trust and deferred assets. It directs revenue to health care, public education, and food assistance through a new special reserve fund.

Direct costs include a $50 million start-up loan to the Franchise Tax Board for administration. Compliance costs for billionaires will be extremely high due to the need for certified appraisals of private businesses, complex debt and liability calculations, and ongoing reporting for those using an Optional Deferral Account. There is also potential opportunity cost if wealthy individuals leave the state or restructure investments to avoid taxation, though the text attempts to limit this through lookback periods.

California residents (and their related trusts) with over $1 billion in net worth pay the tax. The text estimates around 200 billionaires will be affected. Low- and moderate-income Californians, public school students, safety net health care providers, and beneficiaries of food assistance (like CalFresh) benefit from the new dedicated funding streams.

Targeted taxpayers have a strong incentive to move out of California before the 2026 tax obligation date, restructure assets, or transfer wealth into exempt forms (like directly held real estate) or non-taxable trusts. The Franchise Tax Board will likely face intense legal challenges and administrative strain from reviewing certified appraisals and pursuing complex audits. Appraisers face up to 4% penalties for valuation errors, which may increase the cost of their services.

It addresses looming federal and state budget cuts to Medi-Cal, public schools, and food assistance, and rising wealth inequality. The mechanism (a 5% wealth tax on billionaires) directly raises revenue for these specific programs. However, because wealth taxes on illiquid assets are difficult to administer and easy to challenge or evade, the exact revenue yield may fall short of projections.

The Franchise Tax Board gains sweeping powers to appraise wealth, audit billionaires, challenge the Office of Tax Appeals in superior court, and bypass standard rulemaking processes until 2028. The Department of Finance gains discretion in calculating base levels of state appropriations to prevent supplanting.

The behavioral effect of state-level wealth taxes is highly disputed. Some economists argue they lead to massive capital flight and outmigration of the ultra-wealthy, severely reducing the state's tax base and economic investment. Others argue that billionaires are strongly tied to the state's economic ecosystem and that careful design (like taxing trailing wealth or exit taxes) can minimize avoidance and generate substantial revenue.

Administration will be very expensive, as wealth valuation of private businesses and trusts requires specialized audits, legal defenses, and expert appraisers. The measure specifically authorizes the FTB to hire outside counsel and experts on top of a $50 million initial budget.

The measure amends the California Constitution and establishes statutes. The Legislature can amend the statutes with a two-thirds vote, but only if the changes further the measure's purposes. Otherwise, it requires another voter initiative to repeal or substantially alter.

flags.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of the Constitution, the Act provides for taxation on all forms of personal property and wealth
flags.note: Overrides existing constitutional limits on taxing personal property.

flags.quote: The Board shall adopt regulations regarding the taxability of receivables and similar assets under this Part.
flags.note: The actual taxable status of certain financial assets relies on future FTB regulations.

flags.quote: The provisions of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, also referred to as "the Act," are severable.
flags.note: Includes a severability clause and instructions for courts to reform dates or applications to preserve the tax.

flags.quote: An excise tax is imposed for tax year 2026
flags.note: Establishes a specific, one-time application year for the tax.

flags.quote: The Legislature may amend the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, by statute passed in each house of the Legislature by rollcall vote entered in the journal, two-thirds of the membership concurring, if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.
flags.note: Requires a two-thirds vote and limits legislative amendments to those that further the measure's purposes.
